newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's new coffee council vows to boost exports.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's new coffee council vows to boost exports.

text.p: Brazil Friday set up a new coffee council, vowing the body would breath new life into Brazilian coffee policy and return the country to the glory days of the 1970's when it controlled a third of world supply.

Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles, echoed by private sector officials, said one aim of the Conselho Deliberativo da Politica do Cafe (CDPC), or Deliberative Council for Coffee Policy, was to boost exports.

"Brazil must maintain and increase its share (of the world coffee market). We want to raise production from 25 million (60-kg) bags a harvest to 30 million, 35 million bags," he said. "We want to raise our exports."

The minister's bravado was given concrete figures by National Coffee Council (CNC) head Gilson Ximenes, who told reporters Brazil would like to be exporting 19-20 million bags of coffee by the turn of the century.
"We're working on production of 19 million bags this year and want to return to 25 million bags in 1998," Ximenes said.
"But even that's not enough for us to satisfy our objectives of producing 15 million bags for internal consumption and 19-20 million bags for export," he added.
Under an agreement of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC), Brazil's exports in 1996/97 have been limited to 15 million 60-kg bags.

The CDPC consists of 13 members, including the minister as president, and is drawn from the private and the public sectors. It will hold its first formal meeting in Vitoria in the state of Espirito Santo on February 3.
The council was formed on the recommendation of a special parliamentary committee and evolved out of a long-standing complaint by the private sector that Brazilian coffee policy lacked cohesion.

Its brief, according to a statement from the Ministry of Industry and Commerce, will be to approve a yearly crop plan, oversee research into crop estimates and approve government budgets for the sector.
It must also implement programmes to balance demand with supply, establish technical cooperation and financing agreements internationally and decide national coffee stocks policy.

Senator Jose Carlos da Silva Junior of the Association of Brazilian Coffee Industries (ABIC) said he expected the CDPC to quickly adopt a policy of selling off the government's stocks to meet underfed demand, especially from the soluble indutry.
He also reiterated the view, seen by most observers as aimed at domestic media consumption, that the council should seek to boost exports as well as production.
"We are opening a new phase in Brazilian coffee history," da Silva said.
